design_detail: Fixed-effects (within-person) analysis of longitudinal panel data from the Methamphetamine Treatment Evaluation Study (MATES) cohort, Sydney and Brisbane, Australia. 278 people with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence at entry and no lifetime schizophrenia or mania were assessed over four non-contiguous one-month windows (baseline, 3 months, 1 year, 3 years), giving 1064 person-months. Fixed-effects logistic regression related days of methamphetamine use in each month to clinically significant psychotic symptoms in the same month, adjusting for concurrent other drug use.
can_establish: Within the same person, how much more likely clinically significant psychotic symptoms were in months with methamphetamine use than in months without, and how that likelihood scales with days of use, with all stable personal characteristics (sex, heritable traits, personality, premorbid history) removed by design.
cannot_establish: The direction of causation within a month (symptoms and use are measured over the same 4 weeks, so use may follow symptoms as well as precede them); whether methamphetamine use produces lasting vulnerability to psychosis or a psychotic disorder (only symptom presence in four windows was measured); any between-person comparison with non-users (there is no comparison group); and generalization beyond people with methamphetamine dependence, most of them treatment-seeking and injecting.

sample.recruitment: Drawn from the MATES cohort: 400 people entering community-based drug treatment for methamphetamine use in Sydney and Brisbane and 101 people recruited in Sydney through needle and syringe programmes and outreach who screened positive for methamphetamine dependence. Participants were volunteers, reimbursed up to A$40 per interview.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: MATES required age 16 or over, comprehension of English, willingness to be followed up, and no methamphetamine treatment, other inpatient drug treatment or imprisonment in the month before entry (to give a naturalistic baseline). For this analysis, 17 people were excluded for not meeting DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence at recruitment, 59 for meeting DSM-IV criteria for lifetime schizophrenia or a lifetime manic episode, 138 because that diagnostic information was unavailable (they did not take part in the follow-up interviews at which diagnoses were made), and 9 because they used no methamphetamine in any analysed month, leaving 278 of 501.
sample.demographics: Mean age 31.7 years (SD 8.1); 72% men; 72% single; 78% unemployed; 89% Australian-born; 96% English-preferring; median 10 years of schooling (range 6 to 12); 44% with a technical or trade qualification and 6% with a university degree. Mean 13.1 years (SD 7.9) of methamphetamine use and 83% had injected it.
sample.attrition: All 278 were re-interviewed at 3 and 12 months; 230 of 278 (83%) at 3 years, giving 1064 of a possible 1112 person-months (editors' arithmetic: 278 x 3 + 230). Attrition from the parent cohort is larger and selective: 138 of 501 were excluded precisely because they did not attend the follow-up interviews where diagnoses were made.
sample.selection_effects: A dependent, mostly treatment-seeking, mostly injecting sample followed only if they returned for interviews, with people who had a lifetime diagnosis of schizophrenia or mania removed. The authors state the findings should not be generalized to people who use stimulants recreationally or to the general population, and that psychiatric morbidity is particularly high among people who seek drug treatment. The design also requires within-person variation: people whose symptom status never changed across their observed months contribute no information to a fixed-effects logistic model, and the number of participants actually contributing is not reported.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported days of methamphetamine use in the past 4 weeks, measured with the Opiate Treatment Index at each of the four interviews. Self-reported abstinence was checked by hair analysis in a subsample of the wider MATES cohort (n=83), with false reports of abstinence in 6% of cases (reported in the cohort profile paper).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Exposure is frequency, not dose: no use, 1 to 15 days, or 16 to 28 days of use in the past 4 weeks. In months with use, the median was 8 days (range 1 to 28). Main route in months of use was injecting for 79%, smoking 14%, snorting or swallowing 6%. Mean duration of use before entry was 13.1 years. Quantity per occasion and purity were not measured.
exposure.polysubstance: Days of use in the past 4 weeks were recorded for cannabis, heroin, cocaine, ecstasy, hallucinogens, alcohol and tobacco, and entered as time-varying covariates. Use was common: tobacco in 89% of months (median 28 days), cannabis in 57% (median 20 days), alcohol in 62% (median 6 days). Model 1 adjusted for all other drugs; model 2 retained only those with evidence of an association (16 or more days of cannabis or alcohol use).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: abstinence is one of the exposure states. Months of non-use were self-reported, with the 6% false-abstinence rate above as the check.

comparison.controls: Each participant serves as their own control: months with methamphetamine use are compared with months without use in the same person. There is no external comparison group.
comparison.matching: Not applicable. Fixed effects remove all time-invariant characteristics by construction.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Time-invariant premorbid factors are controlled by design, which is the study's central strength. What remains uncontrolled are time-varying factors: the authors name sleep deprivation as a plausible unmeasured one, and note that life stressors could also vary with use.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The within-person comparator months frequently involved tobacco, cannabis and alcohol use; cannabis and alcohol at 16 or more days per month were independently associated with symptoms and were adjusted for.

outcomes.instruments: Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) items for suspiciousness, unusual thought content and hallucinations, rated for the past month by trained interviewers (psychology honours graduates or equivalent) with weekly review meetings to prevent rater drift. 42 interviews were audiotaped and double-rated: agreement 93%, kappa 0.86. Health and social functioning used the 12-Item Short Form physical and mental component scales (disability defined as a score below 40), plus employment, income and accommodation items.
outcomes.validity_norms: A BPRS item score of 4 or more is taken to indicate clinically significant symptom intensity; the same operationalization was used in the group's earlier prevalence work. This is a symptom threshold on an interviewer-rated scale, not a diagnosis of a psychotic disorder, and no diagnostic confirmation of psychosis episodes is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Psychotic symptoms' means a score of 4 or more on any one of the three BPRS items in the past month. Of the months with symptoms, 71% involved suspiciousness, 35% unusual thought content and 51% hallucinations, most in the moderate (4 to 5) rather than severe range.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable to the single outcome; however, nine drug-use predictors were tested, model 2 was built by retaining only variables that showed an association in earlier models, and a further model adding health and social functioning was fitted, all without adjustment.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Interviewers rated symptoms and recorded drug use in the same interview, so ratings were not blind to the participant's reported use in that month.

analysis.effect_sizes: Fixed-effects logistic regression, Stata 11.2, two-sided alpha 0.05. Any methamphetamine use versus none, adjusted (model 2): odds ratio 5.3 (95% CI 3.4 to 8.3), P<0.001. Dose-response, adjusted (model 2): 1 to 15 days versus no use 4.0 (2.5 to 6.5); 16 to 28 days versus no use 11.2 (5.9 to 21.1), both P<0.001. Unadjusted: 4.8 (3.0 to 7.6) and 15.8 (8.6 to 28.7). Model 1 (all other drugs adjusted): 4.2 (2.5 to 7.3) and 12.0 (5.8 to 25.1). Also in model 2: cannabis 16 or more days 2.0 (1.1 to 3.5), P=0.02, and alcohol 16 or more days 2.1 (1.1 to 4.2), P=0.03, both relative to fewer than 16 days. Predicted probabilities from model 2: 7% of months with no methamphetamine use and little cannabis or alcohol; 48% at 16 or more days of methamphetamine use; 61% to 69% when frequent cannabis or alcohol use was added. A further model adjusting for concurrent unemployment, unstable accommodation, low income, psychological distress and physical and mental disability attenuated the estimates to 2.25 (1.29 to 3.90), P=0.004, for 1 to 15 days and 3.90 (1.80 to 8.45), P<0.001, for 16 or more days.
analysis.covariates: Days of use of cannabis, alcohol, tobacco, ecstasy, hallucinogens, cocaine and heroin in the same month (model 1); frequent cannabis and alcohol use only (model 2); and, in a supplementary model, concurrent employment, accommodation, income, psychological distress and disability.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Secondary analysis of an existing cohort (MATES); no registration or analysis plan is referenced.
analysis.selective_reporting: Model 2 is explicitly a post-hoc model retaining only variables that showed an association, and the Table marks the omitted cells as not included. The headline odds ratio of 5.3 for any use versus none appears only in the text and abstract, not in the Table. The number of participants contributing to the fixed-effects estimation (those whose symptom status varied) is not reported. The supplementary model adjusting for health and social functioning is reported in the text only, with two estimates and no full model.
analysis.power: Not discussed. Precision is adequate for the main contrasts (the lower bound for 16 or more days is 5.9) but the heavy-use category rests on 183 of 1064 months, and the attenuated supplementary estimates have wide intervals (1.80 to 8.45).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Within the same people, months in which methamphetamine was used carried about five times the odds of clinically significant psychotic symptoms as months without use, rising to about eleven times in months of use on 16 or more days, after adjusting for concurrent heavy cannabis and alcohol use. In absolute terms the model predicts symptoms in about 7% of abstinent months and about 48% of heavy-use months. Frequent cannabis and alcohol use independently roughly doubled the odds. Adjusting additionally for concurrent unemployment, unstable housing, low income, distress and disability roughly halved the estimates, to about 2.3 and 3.9, while they remained significant.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that there was a large dose-dependent increase in the occurrence of psychotic symptoms during periods of methamphetamine use. That is what the data show. The gaps are narrower than in most papers of this kind, and the discussion itself names several of them: (1) the fixed-effects design removes stable confounding but not time-varying confounding, and sleep deprivation is named as an unmeasured candidate; (2) exposure and outcome are measured over the same month, so within-month direction of effect is not established, as the authors say for cannabis and alcohol, while for methamphetamine they rest the causal direction on external evidence (case reports and experimental administration) rather than on this design; (3) the attenuation to 2.25 and 3.90 after adjusting for concurrent social circumstances is reported as showing that these factors 'could not account for' the association, which is true in the sense of statistical significance but understates a halving of the estimate (those variables may also be consequences of use, so that model may over-adjust); (4) the outcome is a symptom threshold on three BPRS items, not a diagnosis of psychosis; (5) the result applies to people with methamphetamine dependence, which the authors state plainly.

timeline.event: McKetin et al. report the prevalence of psychotic symptoms among people who use methamphetamine, using the same BPRS threshold (cited as reference 8).
McKetin et al. report psychotic symptom risk with recreational methamphetamine use (cited as reference 10).
This study: within-person dose-response in 278 people with dependence, 1064 person-months.
Pooled in the amphetamine mental-health meta-analysis, where it supplies the only adjusted psychosis estimate for any use (odds ratio 5.3)

replication.where_it_stands: The strongest design applied to this question in a human observational sample, and the source of the figure most often cited for methamphetamine and psychotic symptoms. It has not been repeated in an independent cohort with the same within-person method in this reading; the 2019 meta-analysis from an overlapping group carries this study's estimate rather than replicating it, so the two must not be cited as independent support.

funding.funder: National Health and Medical Research Council project grant 350974 and the Australian Government Department of Health and Ageing. The paper states the funders did not participate in design, conduct, data collection, analysis, interpretation, or preparation, review or approval of the manuscript. Data were collected through MATES, conducted by the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales.
funding.declared_conflicts: One author has provided consultancy advice to Lundbeck and received travel support and speaker honoraria from AstraZeneca, Bristol-Myers Squibb, Janssen and Lundbeck; another has received travel support and speaker honoraria from Reckitt Benckiser Pharmaceuticals. No other disclosures are listed.
funding.affiliations_note: Corresponding author at the Centre for Research on Ageing, Health and Well-being, Australian National University; the cohort is an NDARC (UNSW) study. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort with finer temporal resolution (daily or weekly diary or ecological momentary assessment with biological verification) would place use and symptom onset in order within an episode rather than within the same month, and measuring sleep alongside use would test the main unmeasured time-varying confounder; following the same people for years after cessation, with diagnostic interviews rather than a symptom threshold, would show whether a lasting vulnerability to psychotic disorder develops.

domains.note: The fixed-effects design removes all time-invariant confounding, which is the main threat in this literature, and time-varying other drug use is adjusted for. Remaining concerns: unmeasured time-varying confounders (the authors name sleep deprivation), and the supplementary adjustment for concurrent social circumstances halves the estimate, so part of the association travels with circumstances that change alongside use.

Self-reported days of use over the past 4 weeks; hair analysis in a subsample of the parent cohort found 6% false reports of abstinence. Misclassification of abstinent months would, if anything, bias the contrast towards the null. Frequency, not dose, is measured.

278 of 501 in the parent cohort: 138 excluded for not attending follow-up interviews and 59 for lifetime schizophrenia or mania. The analysis also requires within-person variation in the outcome, and the number of participants effectively contributing is not reported. Sample is dependent, mostly treatment-seeking and 83% ever-injecting.

Participants entered drug treatment at baseline, and treatment, medication (including any antipsychotic prescribing) and incarceration during follow-up are not reported as covariates, although they would plausibly change both use and symptoms.
1064 of a possible 1112 person-months observed (96%); 83% retention to 3 years among those included.

Interviewer-rated BPRS with good interrater reliability (kappa 0.86 on 42 double-rated interviews), but raters also collected the drug-use data in the same interview and so were not blind to exposure; the outcome is a three-item symptom threshold over a month, not a diagnosis, and relies on participant recall.
Model 2 retains only covariates that had shown an association; the headline 5.3 estimate is not in the Table; the health and functioning model is reported as two numbers in the text; no protocol.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: For an observational study of this question the design is unusually strong: within-person comparison removes the premorbid confounding that makes the cross-sectional literature uninterpretable, the dose-response is steep and consistent across model specifications, and the outcome measure has documented interrater reliability. What keeps it from low risk is the selected and treatment-seeking sample, the same-month measurement of exposure and outcome, non-blind symptom rating, and the substantial attenuation when concurrent social circumstances are added. The finding is best read as: among people with methamphetamine dependence, psychotic symptoms track their own use closely and in proportion to how much they use.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 278 people with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence and no lifetime schizophrenia or mania, drawn from the 501-person MATES cohort (400 treatment entrants, 101 recruited through needle and syringe programmes and outreach); mean age 31.7 (SD 8.1), 72% men, 78% unemployed, mean 13.1 (SD 7.9) years of use, 83% had injected.
key_findings.locator: Method › Participants and procedure; Results › Characteristics of the sample

key_findings.finding: Design: four non-contiguous one-month observation windows (baseline, 3 months, 1 year, 3 years), 1064 person-months in total; all 278 were re-interviewed at 3 and 12 months and 230 (83%) at 3 years.
key_findings.locator: Method › Participants and procedure, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: Psychotic symptoms (BPRS score of 4 or more on suspiciousness, unusual thought content or hallucinations in the past month) were present in 273 of 1064 months (25%), and 60% of participants reported them in at least one month. Of symptom-months, 71% involved suspiciousness, 35% unusual thought content and 51% hallucinations, mostly in the moderate (4 to 5) range.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of the sample, 3rd paragraph; Table

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine was used in 612 of 1064 months (58%); in those months the median was 8 days of use (range 1 to 28) and injecting was the main route in 79%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of the sample, 2nd paragraph; Table

key_findings.finding: Within-person adjusted association (model 2, adjusting for 16 or more days of cannabis and of alcohol use): any methamphetamine use versus none, odds ratio 5.3 (95% CI 3.4 to 8.3), P<0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Relationship between psychotic symptoms and methamphetamine use, 1st paragraph; Abstract
key_findings.note: This dichotomized estimate appears in the text and abstract only; the Table reports the dose-categorized version.

key_findings.finding: Dose-response (model 2): 1 to 15 days of use versus no use, odds ratio 4.0 (2.5 to 6.5); 16 to 28 days versus no use, 11.2 (5.9 to 21.1); both P<0.001. Unadjusted: 4.8 (3.0 to 7.6) and 15.8 (8.6 to 28.7). Adjusted for all other drug use (model 1): 4.2 (2.5 to 7.3) and 12.0 (5.8 to 25.1).

Absolute risks predicted by model 2: psychotic symptoms in about 7% of months with no methamphetamine use and fewer than 16 days of cannabis or alcohol use, rising to about 48% in months with 16 or more days of methamphetamine use, and to 61% to 69% when frequent cannabis or alcohol use was added.
key_findings.locator: Results, paragraph after the Table; Figure

key_findings.finding: Frequent use of other drugs independently raised the odds: cannabis 16 or more days per month, odds ratio 2.0 (1.1 to 3.5), P=0.02; alcohol 16 or more days, 2.1 (1.1 to 4.2), P=0.03, both relative to fewer than 16 days of that drug. Tobacco, ecstasy, hallucinogen, cocaine and heroin use showed no independent association in the adjusted model.

Adjusting additionally for concurrent unemployment, unstable accommodation, low income, psychological distress and physical and mental disability attenuated the estimates to 2.25 (1.29 to 3.90), P=0.004, for 1 to 15 days and 3.90 (1.80 to 8.45), P<0.001, for 16 or more days.
key_findings.note: Roughly a halving of the main estimates; these covariates may be consequences of use as well as confounders, so this model may over-adjust. The paper describes it as showing these factors could not account for the relationship.

key_findings.finding: Exposure measurement: self-reported days of use in the past 4 weeks (Opiate Treatment Index); in a subsample of the wider cohort (n=83), hair analysis found false reporting of abstinence in 6% of cases.
Outcome reliability: 42 interviews were audiotaped and rated by a second interviewer; agreement for the study definition of psychotic symptoms was 93%, kappa 0.86.

Exclusions from the parent cohort: 17 not meeting dependence criteria, 59 with lifetime schizophrenia or mania, 138 whose diagnostic information was unavailable because they did not take part in the follow-up interviews, and 9 who used no methamphetamine in any analysed month.

The authors state that the findings apply to people with methamphetamine dependence and should not be generalized to people who use stimulants recreationally or to the general population, and that the design does not establish the direction of causality, which they support instead from case reports and experimental administration.

A minority of participants reported psychotic symptoms during abstinent months; the authors offer three readings (a more chronic methamphetamine psychosis, a lasting vulnerability, or subthreshold premorbid psychosis not meeting DSM-IV criteria) and do not distinguish between them.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of participants actually contributing to the fixed-effects estimates is never reported. A fixed-effects logistic model uses only people whose outcome varies across their observed months; with symptoms in 25% of months and 60% of participants ever reporting them, an appreciable share of the 278 can contribute no information.
reporting_issues.consequence: The effective sample behind the odds ratios is smaller than 278 people and 1064 months, and cannot be determined from the paper; precision and generalizability are correspondingly harder to judge.

reporting_issues.issue: In model 2 the cannabis and alcohol odds ratios are relative to fewer than 16 days of use (Table footnote d), while the reference row printed in the Table for those variables is 'no use', which is the reference for the unadjusted column.
reporting_issues.consequence: The cannabis estimate of 2.0 and alcohol estimate of 2.1 are not comparable with the unadjusted estimates of 7.2 and 4.3 in the same row, and should be quoted with their own reference category.

reporting_issues.issue: The headline estimate for any methamphetamine use versus none (odds ratio 5.3, 3.4 to 8.3) appears only in the abstract and text; the Table reports only the three-level dose model.
reporting_issues.consequence: The model behind the most-cited number in the paper cannot be inspected; the dose-categorized estimates in the Table are the auditable ones.

reporting_issues.issue: Model 2 was built by retaining only covariates that had shown evidence of an association in earlier models, and the Table marks the dropped variables with empty cells.
reporting_issues.consequence: The adjusted estimates come from a post-hoc specification; the fully adjusted model 1 estimates (4.2 and 12.0) are close, which limits the practical consequence.

reporting_issues.issue: Symptom ratings and drug-use reports were collected in the same interview by the same interviewer, and blinding is not mentioned.
reporting_issues.consequence: Interviewer knowledge of a participant's reported use in that month could influence BPRS ratings in the direction of the hypothesis.

reporting_issues.issue: The article header gives the online publication as March 2013 while the article information gives 9 January 2013, with the issue citation 2013;70(3):319-324.
reporting_issues.consequence: Bibliographic only; the reference record should use the Crossref dates.
